extracted.intended_audience: literate general readers of The Spectator; readers interested in manners, morals, and social conduct (early-18th-century London audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Short moral/social essays advising on personal conduct, public behaviour, and stylistic propriety; mixes prescriptive maxims with illustrative anecdotes. Aimed at persuading a general readership about good breeding, sincerity, and decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and Plainness
rubrics_metrics.description: The old English Plainness and Sincerity ... generous Integrity of Nature, and Honesty of Disposition ... is in a great measure lost amongst us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sincerity and plainness are superior to affected compliment; the current conversational dialect is swollen with vanity and compliment and has made words 'meer Cyphers'. The essay argues that insincere compliment is harmful because it devalues speech and breeds a habit of dissimulation. Anti-patterns: hollow compliments, habitual flattery; scoring notes: sincerity yields trust and integrity, while dissimulation leads to perpetual suspicion ('When a Man hath once forfeited the Reputation of his Integrity, he is set fast').

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity: be what you seem
rubrics_metrics.description: The best way in the World to seem to be any thing, is really to be what he would seem to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pretence is more troublesome than acquiring the quality itself; the attempt to counterfeit excellency often results in exposure and wasted effort. Artifice tends to disappointment: short-term convenience of falsehood is over, the inconvenience is perpetual. Example/antipattern: assuming qualities by appearance rather than cultivating them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decency/Decorum as a rule of life
rubrics_metrics.description: Decorum, or a Regard to Decency ... carries in it Deference to [others'] good Opinion ... Decency of Behaviour ... obtains the Approbation of all ... from the Order, Consistency, and Moderation of our Words and Actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good breeding equates to observing propriety in dress, speech, and conduct; decency is closely tied to virtue and should be visible in proportionate, moderate behaviour. Violations of decency (excess, inconsistency, disregard for social roles) degrade public esteem. Example guidance: maintain order and moderation; think of virtues as distinct (justice vs modesty) and let modesty prevent offence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility and respect for others' opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: To be negligent of what any one thinks of you, does not only shew you arrogant but abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of good breeding is deference to the judgment of others (humility); this reverence produces social approbation. Anti-pattern: arrogance and disregard for public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of dress and maintaining sex distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: All that needs to be desired of [ladies] is, that they would be themselves, that is, what Nature designed them; ... the Petticoat is a kind of Incumbrance upon [an Amazonian hunting habit], and if the Amazons should think fit to go on ... they ought to add ... wearing the Breeches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid fashionable imitations (especially foreign) that blur natural social distinctions; dress should suit one's sex and social character. Example/antipattern: 'Amazonian' hunting dress for women imported from France is awkward on English modesty — women should present themselves as sister/daughter/wife rather than as romanticized masculine figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation and vain manners
rubrics_metrics.description: The Dialect of Conversation is now-a-days so swelled with Vanity and Compliment ... a certain languishing Vanity appeared in his Air ... his Features ... had a remarkable Effeminacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affectation — exaggerated grooming, foreign airs, and theatrical vanity — harms both individual character and public taste. Example: affectation in personal appearance and speech (over-powdered hair, extravagant dress) is mocked and seen as a sign of superficiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not be a 'mere' something' — avoid intellectual/occupational narrowness (pedantry)
rubrics_metrics.description: A meer Man of the Town ... Bar him the Play-houses ... and you strike him dumb. What are these but rank Pedants? ... a meer Courtier, a meer Soldier, a meer Scholar, a meer any thing, is an insipid Pedantick Character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedantry is not limited to scholars: anyone confined to the narrow circle of their profession or social sphere who cannot think beyond it is a pedant. Anti-patterns: the military pedant (only talks of sieges), law-pedant (always presents cases), state-pedant (wrapt up in newspapers). Prefer conversational breadth over narrow expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance learning with common sense and taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning, like Travelling, and all other Methods of Improvement, as it finishes good Sense, so it makes a silly Man ten thousand times more insufferable, by supplying variety of Matter to his Impertinence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True learning should refine good sense and taste; mere accumulation of books without discernment produces vain, tiresome people. Example/antipattern: scholars who loudly praise trivial editorial corrections or who lack judgment despite many readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clerical and oratorical effectiveness: delivery over needless originality
rubrics_metrics.description: I could heartily wish that more of our Country Clergy would ... endeavour after a handsome Elocution, and all those other Talents that are proper to enforce what has been penned by greater Masters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For preachers, a good aspect, clear voice, graceful delivery, and practical exposition are more edifying than laborious composition of original sermons; abridging and performing great masters' sermons well is preferable. Example: the parish parson who pronounces Tillotson, Barrow, Barrow etc. in an effective series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mastership: humane treatment of servants
rubrics_metrics.description: The Reception, manner of Attendance, undisturbed Freedom and Quiet, which I meet with here in the Country, has confirm'd me in the Opinion I always had, that the general Corruption of Manners in Servants is owing to the Conduct of Masters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Masters set the tone: humane, just, and generous masters foster respectful, cheerful, and loyal servants. Practices include speaking mildly, showing interest in servants' welfare, rewarding service, and arranging independent livelihoods for servants when appropriate. Anti-patterns: harsh masters who provoke flight or servile resentment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate rewards and enabling independence for dependants
rubrics_metrics.description: A good Servant to him is sure of having it in his Choice very soon of being no Servant at all. ... he can often spare a large Fine when a Tenement falls, and give that Settlement to a good Servant who has a Mind to go into the World.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than petty tokens (e.g. passing down cast clothes, which create false equality), reward long service by helping dependants into independent livelihoods (fines, settlements, apprenticeships). This promotes loyalty and social stability; example: sending a coachman's grandson to be an apprentice.
